title: Chile Influenza Activity
text: Chile Influenza Activity is a southern hemisphere influenza signal. In the current U.S. influenza missed-peak failure case, this signal is treated as a candidate hidden driver for the U.S. base influenza mechanism. The graph knowledge says that Chile influenza activity is a LEADING_INDICATOR_FOR U.S. influenza hospitalizations, has an IMPORTATION_LINK to the U.S. influenza base mechanism, and is a POSSIBLE_DRIVER_OF that mechanism. This makes it the strongest current candidate for explaining a missed U.S. hospitalization peak through a lagged importation signal.

title: Australia Influenza Activity
text: Australia Influenza Activity is a southern hemisphere influenza signal. In the current U.S. influenza missed-peak failure case, this signal is a candidate hidden driver because it can act as a leading indicator for U.S. influenza hospitalizations and may be a possible driver of the U.S. influenza base mechanism. The graph knowledge includes LEADING_INDICATOR_FOR and POSSIBLE_DRIVER_OF relationships for this candidate, but it does not include an IMPORTATION_LINK relationship to the U.S. influenza base mechanism.

title: Travel Importation Pressure
text: Travel Importation Pressure is a U.S.-related candidate signal for the missed influenza hospitalization peak. It represents the possibility that travel-driven introductions can increase pressure on the U.S. influenza mechanism. The graph knowledge says this candidate has an IMPORTATION_LINK to the U.S. influenza base mechanism and is a POSSIBLE_DRIVER_OF that mechanism. It is not represented as a LEADING_INDICATOR_FOR the U.S. hospitalization target signal in the current graph.

title: Humidity Drop Anomaly
text: Humidity Drop Anomaly is a climate-related candidate signal for the U.S. influenza missed-peak failure case. It represents a possible environmental forcing that could affect influenza transmission or hospitalization patterns. In the current graph knowledge, Humidity Drop Anomaly is connected to the U.S. influenza base mechanism only through a POSSIBLE_DRIVER_OF relationship. It does not have a LEADING_INDICATOR_FOR relationship to the U.S. hospitalization target signal and does not have an IMPORTATION_LINK relationship to the U.S. influenza base mechanism.

title: US Influenza Base Mechanism
text: The U.S. Influenza Base Mechanism is the mechanism equation being evaluated in the current forecast-failure case. The failure case describes a U.S. influenza model that underpredicted a hospitalization peak. Candidate hidden drivers are evaluated based on whether they can help explain why this base mechanism missed the peak and whether they suggest a testable model edit, such as adding an external lagged importation signal.

title: US Hospitalizations Target Signal
text: U.S. Influenza Hospitalizations is the target signal in the current missed-peak failure case. The model failure is defined by actual U.S. hospitalizations rising above the forecast. Candidate hidden drivers are more relevant when they help explain this target signal, especially when they are represented as leading indicators or possible drivers of the U.S. influenza mechanism.

title: Candidate Scoring Rule
text: The current candidate scoring rule favors graph evidence that connects a candidate signal to the failed U.S. influenza mechanism and the U.S. hospitalization target signal. A LEADING_INDICATOR_FOR relationship to the target signal contributes the strongest evidence. IMPORTATION_LINK and POSSIBLE_DRIVER_OF relationships to the U.S. influenza base mechanism also increase support. A candidate with all three relationships is expected to rank above candidates with only one or two of these relationships.

title: Southern Hemisphere Surveillance Background
text: Southern hemisphere influenza surveillance can provide useful context for northern hemisphere preparedness because influenza seasons occur at different times across regions. These surveillance signals may suggest broad seasonal pressure, but surveillance context alone is not enough to establish a specific driver relationship for a U.S. model failure. Additional evidence is needed before treating any regional signal as a concrete explanation for a missed hospitalization peak.

title: Travel Volume Seasonality
text: Travel volume can vary by season, holidays, and school calendars. Higher travel volume may increase opportunities for respiratory virus introductions, but travel volume alone does not identify which pathogen signal is leading the U.S. hospitalization target. Travel-related context should be combined with candidate-specific evidence before proposing a model edit.

title: Humidity and Respiratory Transmission Background
text: Humidity can affect respiratory virus transmission conditions, including viral stability and host susceptibility. A humidity anomaly may be relevant as environmental context, but environmental plausibility is not the same as complete support for a hidden driver. A climate-related signal should not be treated as fully explanatory unless it has direct evidence linking it to the target failure and mechanism.

title: US Hospitalization Reporting Lag
text: Hospitalization data can be affected by reporting delays, revisions, and week-to-week noise. A missed hospitalization peak may sometimes reflect delayed reporting or data revision rather than a missing epidemiological driver. Reporting lag should be considered as a data-quality explanation, but it is not itself evidence for a specific candidate hidden driver.

title: Generic Model Underprediction Explanation
text: An epidemiological model can underpredict a peak for several reasons, including missing external inputs, incorrect parameter values, reporting artifacts, behavioral changes, or changes in population susceptibility. A useful revision should identify which mechanism is under-supported and propose a testable edit rather than simply naming a plausible factor.

title: Noisy Candidate Signal Warning
text: Candidate signals can be noisy, correlated, or temporally misaligned with the target failure. A signal that appears plausible in narrative form may still be weak if it lacks specific support for timing, mechanism connection, or target relevance. Ranking should avoid over-weighting a candidate merely because its description resembles the failure pattern.

title: Incomplete Evidence Warning
text: Incomplete evidence occurs when a candidate has one or two relevant support relationships but lacks another relationship needed for full support. In these cases, the candidate may still be relevant, but it should be described as partially supported rather than as the best complete explanation. Missing relationships should be stated explicitly when evaluating a candidate.

title: External Driver Model Edit Background
text: A model edit that adds an external driver should be based on evidence that the driver is relevant to the failed target signal and connected to the mechanism being revised. External inputs can be represented as lagged covariates, forcing terms, or seeding terms, but the edit should remain testable and should not imply confirmed causality without validation.
